title: A life by conditions
hook: from conception to awakening, a whole life traced by causes

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sati's mistake, and your line, from conditions. Did you catch one mood and see what it was burning? Today, the end of a week, and the same discourse, zoomed all the way out. Day four hundred thirty-four.

Baby photos are strange things. There you are, a few days old, red-faced and furious, and somehow that's you. Then a kid on a tricycle. Then a teenager with that haircut. The album asks a question without saying it: how did that one become this one? Near the end of yesterday's discourse, the Buddha answers it. He walks through an entire human life, from before birth to freedom, and shows each step resting on the one before. Today: a life by conditions.
screen: `A BABY PHOTO. A TRICYCLE. THAT HAIRCUT.` → `HOW DID THAT ONE BECOME THIS ONE?` → `A WHOLE LIFE, STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: This is the second half of the thirty-eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. It begins before birth. A life begins, the text says, when three things come together: the mother and father unite, the mother is in season, and a being to be born is present. Not one condition, three. Then the mother carries the child nine or ten months, with great anxiety, and nourishes it after birth with her own milk. The discourse says that in this teaching, mother's milk is called blood. Then the child grows, and the text lists children's games: toy plows, little carts, bows and arrows, somersaults, a game with sticks. Then the adult, enjoying the five kinds of sense pleasure. Seeing a pleasant sight, they lean toward it. An unpleasant one, they lean away. Feeling becomes delight, delight becomes clinging, clinging becomes being, and on rolls the wheel of birth, aging and death. Then the turn. A Buddha appears in the world. The person hears the teaching, gains trust, and trains: virtue, guarding the senses, mindfulness, stillness. Now, seeing a sight, they don't lean. Feeling arises, and no delight hooks it. Without delight, no clinging. Without clinging, the wheel stops. Every stage, the baby, the child, the craving adult and the free one, comes from conditions. That's the hope in it. If the knot was tied by causes, it can be untied by causes. Look back at the week: a grove lit many ways, a cowherd's craft, a debater's sweat, a childhood tree, a trembling palace, a fire and its fuel. All of it, from conditions.
screen: `THREE THINGS, AND A LIFE BEGINS` · `CHILDHOOD GAMES, THEN SENSE PLEASURE` · `FEELING, DELIGHT, CLINGING, BIRTH` · `THE TURN: NO DELIGHT, NO CLINGING` · then, large: `ALL FROM CONDITIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace one life event's causes. Pick something real that happened to you: a move, a friendship, a job, a loss. Sit, and ask what made it possible. Not one cause: look for three or four. A person you met. A choice you made. Something that happened before you were born. Let each condition appear, and see how none of them alone was enough. Then let it all settle back into the breath, itself coming from conditions. The bell holds the time.
A life by conditions. From conception to childhood, craving and freedom, every stage resting on causes, so every knot can be untied. Today's word.
Your line: all from conditions. Today, when someone frustrates you, remember they too were a baby with games and hungers, shaped by causes. Day four hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers present dependent origination (paticca samuppada) as a chain of conditions, painted in Tibetan temple art as the wheel of life; MN 38 gives it as a human life, from conception and childhood to the release that comes when craving ends.

match.prompt: a life, step by step — tap the pairs.
pairs: no clinging, and the wheel stops

myth: the discourse says a life begins from one single cause
it names three things that must come together, and each later stage rests on others.
MN 38 lists children's games like toy plows and somersaults
the Buddha walks through childhood in ordinary detail before reaching the adult and craving.
in the discourse, the wheel stops when feeling stops
feeling still arises; it stops when no delight hooks the feeling, so clinging doesn't follow.

fork.setup: you've heard the teaching and trained. you see a beautiful sight, and a pleasant feeling arises. according to MN 38, what happens next for the trained one?
options: the feeling arises, but no delight hooks it.
nothing: they no longer see sights.
fork.reveal: the trained one still sees and feels. what changes is that delight doesn't seize the feeling, and without delight there's no clinging.

original.note: Pali paticca samuppada: dependent origination, things arising by way of conditions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a life is one long thing that just happens to you.
what it means: each stage rests on conditions, which is why the knot of craving can be untied.
what a scholar hears: MN 38 frames the whole life story inside dependent origination, and the discourse's title, the destruction of craving, names what breaks the chain.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 38, Mahatanhasankhaya Sutta (the greater discourse on the destruction of craving), later section

notes: MN 38 paraphrased: three conditions for conception (union of parents, mother in season, the gandhabba present: rendered 'a being to be born'), nine or ten months, milk called blood, children's games, sense pleasures, the chain to birth and death, the trained disciple. Confirm each detail and the list of games.
The Tibetan wheel of life (bhavacakra) mentioned only in howItsDone as a general description.
